title: Ghost Shift - Our 4th game made with heavy AI use
author: Slackluster
selftext:
# GHOST SHIFT

*The art is fake but the danger is real*

# [Play Ghost Shift on itch.io](https://focaccai.itch.io/ghost-shift)

Ghost Shift is an interactive adventure game set in a museum basement during a night shift. You play as Mara, a contract specialist who uncovers art fraud. Every page ends with a simple choice. Pick wrong and you fall into a dead end that parodies a different scifi trope like Her, Terminator, The Matrix, Westworld, System Shock, etc.

Rather than making one large complex game, our strategy has been to create many short games and focus on improving the story and core experience with each one. This game took only about 3 days, leveraging some of the tools we already built for previous games.

The whole thing was built with AI tools and a human creative director. Here's how...

# The Story

The plot came from Claude. I asked for pitches and got two I liked. One about a forensic accountant investigating a fintech startup, and another about a museum digitization specialist finding catalog errors. I told Claude to combine them, add real stakes, make the boss the villain, and use the AI system to save the protagonist rather than be the enemy. Claude came up with the rest, including the characters Mara, Linden, and SOLA, which I kept.

From there it was many revision passes. I would provide feedback, ask for a rewrite, and ask Claude to give its own feedback. We went through over 10 full revisions and every one required human direction. AI is great at structure and first drafts but still needs a lot of handholding. It doesn't know what to cut, it struggles with humor, and it tends to over explain. My job was mostly knowing when to remove things.

The main story spine is grounded and realistic, but the dead-ends let us go wild with a different crazy scifi trope on each one. My favorite is actually the first dead end where everyone just becomes friends with the AI. It makes me laugh every time.

# The Art

We wanted an art style that didn't look like stereotypical AI art. So we experimented with over 20 art styles by sending the same prompt through different style modifiers to find ones that are more interesting. If you want to replicate the look, the key ingredient is: "vintage educational game screenshot"

Claude wrote the detailed image prompts for composition, camera angle, lighting, and mood. Each prompt includes character and scene info to keep things consistent across pages. From there it's a quick automated step to generate the images with gpt-image-1.5. I cherry-picked and regenerated some to get the best versions.

# The Cover

For the cover we went in a different direction than the ingame art, leaning into the nostalgia to create vintage box art.

We started with ChatGPT to get a cheesy scholastic kind of look, the sort of thing you'd see on a cheap paperback. Then we used Nano Banana 2 to place that game box in a museum setting. Mixing models like this was an experiment to get more unique image results.

# The Music

The music is an instrumental track generated with Suno v4.5. I gave Claude the full story and some ideas about tone and it wrote several prompts I could feed to Suno. From there it just took some iteration to arrive at the final track.

# What We've Learned After 4 Games

The biggest difference between game one and game four is that our process is more iterative and seamless now. We focus on getting the core story working well before moving on to prose refinement, image gen, or anything else.

The most frustrating thing is that AI still needs constant human feedback. The most surprising thing is how much of the creative work it can do when you give it good direction. Most of the plot and story are Claude's. I just helped steer and gave it a few key ideas.

If you want to try making something like this, my best advice is to keep it simple. Focus on making something small and good.

# The Stack

* Story and Prompts: Claude Opus 4.6
* Cover Image: Nano Banana 2
* Page Images: gpt-image-1.5
* Music: Suno v4.5
* Automation: node.js

Is this the kind of tool you'd like access to? We hope to make a version publicly available someday. Let us know what you think.

comments.author: LogDoubtDev
comments.body: Looks cool, I like the art.  Do you use any post processing on the images, or what kind of prompt did you use to get that pixelated style?

replies.author: Slackluster
replies.body:
thanks! we did not use post processing for images, though it is something i want to explore with future games. i think we could use webgl to do some really cool effects, animations, and transitions.

the key words for the art prompt are: "vintage educational game screenshot" you will need to play around with it to get the exact vibe you want.

replies.body: Haha nice!  I never thought of using that kind of concept for a prompt. Just took me back to 4th grade core memory of Carmen San Diego.

comments.author: hblok
comments.body:
Why does the text have to show up word by word, line by line?

Surely that's last-year by now?

replies.author: Slackluster
replies.body:
the text display effect is part of the design. it adds some vibe of traditional narrative driven games while also setting the pace. it is fast enough that people will not be slowed down if they are just skimming the text. the code behind the effect could still stand to be improved though.

how would you do it better?

replies.author: hblok
replies.body:
>traditional narrative driven games

No game I ever played which displayed similar amounts of text had the words pop up one by one. The exception is maybe the odd "secret code" or other small messages coming through an old modem, tele-prompt or similar system.

However, beyond the fact that there's no precedence for it, what really has made this style dated is the last couple of years of AI responses to prompts. It has just become the epitome of extremely poor user design. For most AI responses, a spinner would have been better. The response gradually coming in, and then eventually failing to render properly, so I have to refresh the page anyway is just infuriating. (But of course, not your fault, and not a problem in your game).  
  
However, it still seems to me that that's not a feeling you want to evoke in the game you're making.

Furthermore, I guess there are other reasons for why you would not want to impede the user and dictate the speed or style they should read by. E.g. Maybe they've already read it.  
  
So make it simple. Just display the full text at once.

replies.author: Slackluster
replies.body:
thanks for your feedback, i will think on it. in the debug mode the text appears instantly but it feels cheaper.

it seems to me like most rpgs and interactive novels work this way by displaying letters on at a time. Take Legend of Zelda, Breath of the wild for example. Maybe it is because in a game like that you click through a few sentences at a time while in my game it displays the whole page?

now i am thinking maybe the real problem is the display should be broken up, so instead of showing the full page, it shows one paragraph at a time while the user clicks through.

something else about my game is not coming through though. there is no AI responses or prompts. everything has already been generated and gone through many revision passes.

replies.author: hblok
replies.body:
Right, right. I get that's it not an AI generated response.

However, that was my point. The gradually revealing text will most easily be associated with AI response today. And for me at least, I'm not the least found of it.

But yeah, maybe doing a paragraph at a time works better.

replies.author: Slackluster
replies.body:
thanks for your input, i really appreciate it. i actually spent a while making changes to address this. if you have a few minutes could you load up a page or 2 and see if this flow feels better?

basically it shows 1 paragraph at a time, and i also did a slight rewrite to accommodate the new flow better. 

[https://focaccai.itch.io/ghost-shift](https://focaccai.itch.io/ghost-shift)

replies.author: ZHName
replies.body:
Look Dragon Quest Reimagined is stellar: it uses letter-by-letter typeout effect in dialogue. Totally fine to do it this way or by word or by sentence. It's style.

I actually have a few other points for you to consider in future games:

1) can you add clickable areas on the pictures? this will elevate each page to where the player can choose what they can learn from the scene. This is challenging to implement but would add immersion since this is a narrative driven game.

2) can you add subtle vocals like "uh huh" or "okay" etc using elevenlabs for your main character so that there's a connectedness with audio-and character. (this is a small quality increase)

3) I found the endings to be too abrupt on a number of them. Maybe you're spread too thin and didn't polish the best storylines you want in the game. The more satisfying endings need an intriguing twist or clear indication of what happened -- "you died", or "you're fired and the professor is injured leading to dishonor" -- I couldn't tell what the endings suggested because they were too vague at times. Choose your own adventure books vary in their approaches but I'm pretty sure being crystal clear about the game over statement is important here.

4) can you add a simple mini game mechanic that is reusable in your game? Think along the lines of a fallout lock. It's a simple mechanic but adds something. Pair it with some rng items you can unlock..... this might be your mystery spice to increase fun in this narrative-action game.

replies.author: Slackluster
replies.body:
thanks for your feedback!

i plan to add more depth to future games while continue to iterate on these current games. that can include things like clicking on images, mini games, and more complex branching.

vocal cues is a great idea. id like to add full voiceover at some point but even just a few voice sounds could add a lot, also sound effects at key story points.

for my next game the goal is to not have any dead ends, we'll see how it goes.

mini games could also be great. i was also thinking how it would be fun in this game to control the robot arm. i'll think about how i could add in a segment like that.
